h: פָּרָשַׁת זָכוֹר, מַאֲמָר א׳ Parshas Zachor — Maamar Aleph

p: זָכוֹר אֵת אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה לְךָ עֲמָלֵק
how he happened upon you on the way, etc."
why "on the way" is said twice.
Also, what is the meaning of the remembering,
and what did he tell them?
Did not the generation of the wilderness know it on their own,
being members of the very generation he fought against?
he flew like a creeping locust
Amalek, who came to lick up
the blood of Yisrael like a dog.
That is, he is called Amalek
on account of the two matters mentioned above.
That he flew like a locust
וּבָא לַעֲשׂוֹת מִלְחָמָה עִם יִשְׂרָאֵל וְכוּלֵּי
and he came to make war with Yisrael, etc."
In its plain sense, he lived far away from Eretz Yisrael,
a distance of four hundred parsa.
But it may be said that the intent is
that it alludes to the kelipah of Amalek,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (זֹהַר שְׁלַח חֵלֶק ג קס, א).
בְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר שֶׁהָיָה מִתְלוֹצֵץ בְּעוֹבְרֵי עֲבֵירָה וְכוּלֵּי
regarding Rabbi Meir, who would mock transgressors, etc.:
were it not that they proclaim in Heaven,
'Be careful with Rabbi Meir and his Torah,' etc."
So the evil inclination was able to come
and entice Rabbi Meir to a matter of sin,
that he would illuminate the eyes of the Sages in halachah.
בְּרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא שֶׁהָיָה מִתְלוֹצֵץ בְּעוֹבְרֵי עֲבֵירָה
regarding Rabbi Akiva, that he would mock transgressors,
and it sought to make him stumble as well,
and it said, "Were it not that they proclaim in Heaven,
'Be careful with Rabbi Akiva and his Torah,' etc."
And this, even though they said
(מִדְרָשׁ חֻקַּת רַבָּה יט, ו; תַּנְחוּמָא ח)
כָּל יְקָר רָאֲתָה עֵינוֹ [אִיּוֹב כח, י]
"'His eye has seen every precious thing' (Iyov 28:10) —
this is Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues;
things that were not revealed to Moshe
were revealed to Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues."
And he was the root of Torah she'b'al peh,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ כַּמָּה פְּעָמִים מֵהָאֲרִ״י זַ״ל.
as we have said several times in the name of the Arizal.
to entice him to a matter of sin,
had they not been guarded from Above.
וְעַל זֶה רוֹמֵז אֲשֶׁר קָרְךָ בַּדֶּרֶךְ
And to this alludes "how he happened upon you on the way":
that it was like a chance occurrence,
דָּבָר אֲשֶׁר לֹא יַעֲלֶה עַל לֵב
a thing that would not enter one's mind.
they were certainly far removed from this matter,
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא נִתְבַּיֵּישׁ הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע
and nonetheless the evil inclination was not ashamed
to come at them to seduce them.
"Be careful of me on account of my daughter,"
even though seclusion with her is permitted.
And it seems that this was
for beforehand he would mock transgressors.
who scoffed at Rabbi Tarfon (Kiddushin there)
was presumably far from any matter of desire,
before that student stumbled with his mother-in-law";
And to this alludes what it says,
עֲמָלֵק יוֹשֵׁב בְּאֶרֶץ הַנֶּגֶב [בַּמִּדְבָּר יג, כט],
"Amalek dwells in the land of the Negev" (Bamidbar 13:29),
That is, it dwells in the "land of the Negev,"
וּמְרַמֵּז שֶׁנִּכְנָס אַף לְלֵב קָדוֹשׁ כָּזֶה
alluding that it enters even such a holy heart
that is dried out of all craving and desire,
"'You have given me the land of the Negev' (Yehoshua 15:19) —
a house dried out of all good, etc.,
אָדָם שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ אֶלָּא תּוֹרָה בִּלְבַד
a man in whom there is nothing but Torah alone"
זָכוֹר אֵת אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה לְךָ עֲמָלֵק
on the way, when you went out of Egypt":
that is, after they had gone out
from all ten crowns of impurity
through the ten plagues that corresponded to them,
and they entered into the ten holinesses, the ten Sefiros,
and they merited, through the plague of the firstborn,
to be bound to the root,
and they were then called "My son, My firstborn, Yisrael"
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם יָכוֹל עֲמָלֵק לְהִזָּוֵוג לָהֶם.
and nonetheless Amalek was able to attach himself to them.
And it says, "how he happened upon you on the way" —
on which they were going to receive the Torah from Sinai.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא נִתְבַּיֵּישׁ לְהִזְדַּוֵּוג לָכֶם
And nonetheless he was not ashamed to attach himself to you,
though it was a chance occurrence
that would not be believed if told.
that a person should beware of the seductions of the evil inclination
and not rely on his greatness,
וּכְהָא דִּתְנַן [אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק ב מִשְׁנָה ד]
as we learned in the Mishnah (Avos 2:4):
אַל תַּאֲמִין בְּעַצְמְךָ עַד יוֹם מוֹתְךָ
"Do not trust yourself until the day of your death,"
for then they are certainly truly complete;
for all the days of a man
he is in the aspect of "going,"
to be refined in his attribute,
which is his "eternal home" designated for him,
until the day of his death,
so that he can no longer spoil it,
וְאֵין לוֹ עֵסֶק עוֹד בָּזֶה הָעוֹלָם
and he has no more business in this world,
וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמַר מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
This is in the manner of what Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him, said:
[דְּבָרִים לא, ב] לֹא אוּכַל עוֹד לָצֵאת וְלָבֹא.
(Devarim 31:2) "I can no longer go out and come in."
וּבִירוּשַׁלְמִי (שַׁבָּת פֶּרֶק א הֲלָכָה ג, ח, א)
regarding a pious man who would teach:
אַל תַּאֲמֵן בְּעַצְמְךָ עַד יוֹם זִקְנוּתְךָ
"Do not trust yourself until the day of your old age,"
And she said, "Change it for your fellows,
to teach 'until the day of your death,'"
And for this comes the mitzvah to remember
to attach himself to them on the way
in the aspect of "turn from evil,"
and on the way on which they went to receive the Torah,
so that a person, even when he is
at a supreme level of holiness and purity,
of the seductions of the evil inclination,
וְעַל שֵׁם זֶה נִקְרָא עַם יֶלֶק
And on account of this he is called "a people of yelek,"
who flew like a locust from four hundred parsa,
alluding that even one who is distant from his kelipah
and dried out of all craving and desire,
as the measure of four hundred parsa,
the measure of the entire land —
he nonetheless flies to him like a locust.
He is further called Amalek because
שֶׁבָּא לָלוֹק דָּמָן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל כְּכֶלֶב
he came to lick up the blood of Yisrael like a dog,
and this is what it says,
"And he struck at your rear, all the stragglers, etc."
and it is stated (in Pesikta Rabbasi
לְפָרָשַׁת זָכוֹר פָּרָשָׁה יב סִימָן יג
And into them he brought despair
and through this he seduced them,
עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמַר אַחֵר (חֲגִיגָה טו, א)
in the manner of what Acher said (Chagigah 15a):
"Since that man has been driven out
let him go out and enjoy this world."
וְכָל כָּךְ גּוֹרֵר אוֹתָם הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע
The evil inclination drags them so far
that it brings them to extreme brazenness.
This is what they said in the Pesikta (for Chanukah, parsha 7)
what the nature of the 'zemorah' was,
until Amalek came and taught it to them,
'And behold, they put forth the zemorah, etc.'
And from whom did he learn it?
he cleared his throat and put forth the zemorah" —
and this has no clear explanation.
the verse is said about their standing
"with their backs toward the Sanctuary of Hashem,"
as a sound coming out from their rear
and so it appears from the Targum.
לֹא הָיָה אוֹפֶן שֶׁיִּהְיֶה נִמְצָא בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל
was not something that could be found in Yisrael;
rather, it was Amalek who brought in this brazenness,
and he, though he heard and knew everything,
And this he learned from Esav his grandfather,
who, even though he was very troubled about the blessings
with which Yaakov was blessed by his father,
nonetheless scoffed at it all entirely,
cleared his throat and put forth the zemorah.
refer to Amalek, who was a scoffer.
And this is the matter of heresy.
And this he brought into Yisrael,
so that they came to this brazenness,
בְּמַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר וְהִנָּם שׁוֹלְחִים אֶת הַזְּמוֹרָה וְגוֹמֵר.
as it says, "And behold, they put forth the zemorah, etc."
This is the way of the evil inclination:
when it sees that a person has stumbled in some sin
through its counsel and its seduction,
it afterwards casts him into despair,
saying, "What will your teshuvah help you,
אַחַר כִּי גָּדוֹל עֲוֹנְךָ עַד לַשָּׁמַיִם
since your sin is so great, reaching to the heavens?
And since that man has been driven out
let him go out and enjoy this world."
וְעַל שֵׁם זֶה נִקְרָא עֲמָלֵק עַם לָק
And on account of this he is called Amalek, "am lak,"
שֶׁבָּא לָלוֹק דָּמָן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל כְּכֶלֶב
who came to lick up the blood of Yisrael like a dog,
who came to suck out the remnant of their blood and vitality
to the very end, as mentioned above.
וּבָא הַמִּצְוָה תִּמְחֶה אֶת זֵכֶר עֲמָלֵק
And the mitzvah "You shall erase the memory of Amalek" comes
namely, that even one who is great in stature
should not rely on his holiness,
and should beware of the seductions of the evil inclination;
וְאַף מִי שֶׁנִּכְשַׁל חַס וְשָׁלוֹם מַה
and even one who has stumbled in something, Heaven forbid,
but should return to Hashem, and He will have mercy on him.
וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ (תַּנְחוּמָא כִּי תֵצֵא ד)
And regarding this they said (Tanchuma, Ki Seitzei 4):
The Holy One, blessed be He, said to them:
and I will erase his name above, etc."
And this is what it says,
"Hashem will not leave him in his hand,"
שֶׁנִּדְרָשׁ (סוּכָּה נב, ב) עַל הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע
which is expounded (Sukkah 52b) about the evil inclination:
were it not that the Holy One, blessed be He, helps him,
"and Hashem will not leave him in his hand."
which is expounded in the Pesikta
for this is the main root of the evil inclination,
and I created Torah as its antidote";
for Hashem Yisbarach created this inclination
to be for good, a longing for words of Torah,
through the seduction of the serpent,
which was through desire in eating,
and afterwards he injected filth into Chavah
and the filth clung to Adam HaRishon and his offspring.
"The Holy One, blessed be He, called it 'evil'";
that is, the inclination of lust
of the generation of the Flood,
for one who blemishes in this is called "evil in the eyes of Hashem,"
as they said in the Zohar HaKadosh
that whoever is greater than his fellow,
his inclination is greater than he (Sukkah there);
"Had it been one who hates me,
he would not have been able to restrain himself"
And this is what it says, "how he happened upon you on the way."
"I have remembered what Amalek did to Yisrael,
how he set upon him on the way, etc."
Now if it refers to the war,
have not many always oppressed us?
And the Greeks decreed religious persecution
in the days of the Chashmona'im, more than Amalek did.
אַךְ הָעִיקָּר מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר אַחַר כָּךְ
But the main thing is what is said afterwards,
"how he happened upon you on the way":
that he defiled you, as mentioned above;
"and he struck at your rear, all the stragglers":
that he brought despair into the stragglers,
וְזֶה עִנְיַן מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת קיח, ב)
And this is the meaning of what they said (Shabbos 118b):
no nation or tongue would have ruled over them,
'And it was on the seventh day,
and right after it is written (there 17:8),
At first glance this is not understood,
דְּהָא עֲמָלֵק לֹא שָׁלַט בָּהֶם כְּלָל,
for Amalek did not rule over them at all,
And after the wars Rachav testified,
וְלֹא קָמָה עוֹד רוּחַ בְּאִישׁ מִפְּנֵיכֶם
and no spirit remained any longer in any man because of you"
וְאַחַר כָּךְ נִכְנְסוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל לְאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל
And afterwards Yisrael entered Eretz Yisrael,
and the Beis HaMikdash was built,
and there were the days of Shlomo,
and all the days of the First Temple,
אַךְ הָעִיקָּר אֲשֶׁר שָׂם לוֹ בַּדֶּרֶךְ
But the main thing is "how he set upon him on the way":
Amalek brought despair into those who stumbled,
and through this he dragged them along
until he came to lick up the remnant of their blood
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה גָּרַם לָהֶם עֲמָלֵק הַשִּׁעְבּוּד
and through this Amalek caused them the subjugation
that came afterwards, a long time later.
For were it not for the war of Amalek
and the despair he brought into their hearts,
Yisrael would have remained in the same state
they were in at Matan Torah,
and they would never have been spoiled.
Only Amalek caused it for them,
and afterwards the despair, as mentioned above.
וְזֶה גָּרַם מַה שֶּׁלֹּא שָׁמְרוּ שַׁבָּת רִאשׁוֹנָה.
And this is what caused them not to keep the first Shabbos.
"You shall erase the memory of Amalek,"
through our mentioning his name below,
and Hashem Yisbarach erases his name above
for one who comes to purify himself is given help.
And this is the meaning of reading the parsha
that through this we will merit
to carry out the eradication of Amalek properly.
And we mention his name on the Shabbos before it
so that we will merit the eradication of Amalek on Purim,
and immediately be redeemed in Nissan

paragraphs.text: Deuteronomy 25:17–19 — “Remember what Amalek did to you on the way when you came out of Egypt: how he encountered you on the way and struck at your rear, all the stragglers behind you, while you were weary and exhausted; he did not fear God. When Hashem your God grants you rest from all your enemies around you, in the land that Hashem your God gives you as an inheritance to possess, you shall blot out Amalek's remembrance from beneath the heavens. Do not forget.” Rav Tzadok's opening questions concern the two occurrences of 'on the way,' the need to remember an event known to its witnesses, and the distinction between remembering and blotting out.

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Ki Seitzei 9; Targum Yonasan on Nachum 3:16 — “What is Amalek? A people that licks, flying like a locust. Amalek: a people that came to lick up Israel's blood like a dog. ... It was taught in Rabbi Nassan's name: Amalek traversed four hundred parasangs and came to make war against Israel at Refidim, as it says, 'Amalek dwells in the land of the Negev.'” The checked text reads am lak, 'a people that licks'; Rav Tzadok also hears am yelek, a people likened to a locust. He treats the locust's reach and the dog's licking as two different spiritual dangers, rather than merely two descriptions of the same attack. Targum Yonasan on Nachum 3:16 renders the verse's yelek as zachala: 'You increased your merchants beyond the stars of heaven; behold, like a locust that casts off its covering and flies.' This is a precise example of the gloss Rav Tzadok supplies.

paragraphs.text: Kiddushin 81a — “Rabbi Meir would mock transgressors. One day Satan appeared to him as a woman on the other bank of a river. There was no ferry; he seized a rope and began crossing. When he reached the middle of the rope, Satan left him and said: 'Were it not that they proclaim in Heaven, Beware of Rabbi Meir and his Torah, I would have made your blood worth two ma'ah.'” The episode makes protection from temptation dependent on help from above even for a great sage.

paragraphs.text: Eruvin 13b — “It was taught: His name was not Rabbi Meir, but Rabbi Nehorai. Why was he called Rabbi Meir? Because he illuminated the eyes of the Sages in halachah. And his name was not Nehorai, but Rabbi Nechemyah—or, some say, Rabbi Elazar ben Arach. Why was he called Nehorai? Because he enlightened the eyes of the Sages in halachah.” The statement establishes Rabbi Meir's extraordinary illuminating power in Torah. Rav Tzadok emphasizes that this greatness did not make vigilance unnecessary.

paragraphs.text: Kiddushin 81a — “Rabbi Akiva would mock transgressors. One day Satan appeared to him as a woman at the top of a palm tree. He took hold of the tree and began climbing. When he reached halfway up, Satan left him and said: 'Were it not that they proclaim in Heaven, Beware of Rabbi Akiva and his Torah, I would have made your blood worth two ma'ah.'” This is the companion episode to Rabbi Meir's, with a different obstacle and the same heavenly protection. Rav Tzadok cites both as evidence that no level of learning makes a person independent of Divine aid.

paragraphs.text: Pri Tzaddik, Lag BaOmer 1 — “Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him, was the root of Torah she'bichsav, and Rabbi Akiva was the root of Torah she'b'al peh (as is stated in the writings of the Arizal).” Rav Tzadok states the teaching outright there, attributing it to the Arizal's writings, and he refers to it again in Parshas Zachor, Maamar Yud Bais, and Parshas Parah, Maamar Bais. The Arizal's teaching is in Pri Etz Chaim, Shaar Rosh Chodesh, chapter 3: Yitzchak loved Esav “because the hunt was in his mouth” for the sake of the holy spark within him, which drew from the three highest levels, the heads of Yisrael such as Shemayah and Avtalyon, Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Akiva. Rav Tzadok himself joins the two in Ohr Zarua LaTzaddik 5: “Moshe Rabbeinu is the foundation of Torah she'bichsav and Rabbi Akiva the foundation of Torah she'b'al peh; he was a descendant of converts and came from Esav, as is known from the Arizal on ‘because the hunt was in his mouth,’ and this is the secret of Torah she'b'al peh.” Compare also Asarah Maamaros, Chakor Din 5:11, and Megaleh Amukos, Va'eschanan, ofen 72.

paragraphs.text: Kiddushin 81b — “Rabbi Meir said: 'Be careful with me because of my daughter.' Rabbi Tarfon said: 'Be careful with me because of my daughter-in-law.' A student mocked him. Rabbi Abbahu said in the name of Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel: Before many days had passed, that student stumbled with his mother-in-law.” The passage follows a discussion of seclusion with close relatives. Rav Tzadok reads the sages' caution as refusing to presume immunity, and the student's failure as the danger of scoffing at such caution. The suggestion that Rabbi Meir's warning followed the earlier episode is Rav Tzadok's inference; the Gemara does not date the two incidents.

paragraphs.text: Temurah 16a — “She said: 'Give me a blessing, for you have given me the land of the Negev'—a house dried out of every good thing. 'Give me springs of water'—a man who possesses nothing but Torah. 'Kalev gave her upper springs and lower springs.' He said to her: 'Would one in whom the upper and lower worlds dwell ask me for sustenance?'” The Gemara expounds Achsah's request to Kalev after her marriage to Osniel. Rav Tzadok takes its wordplay on Negev and menuggav, 'dried out,' as a model for describing a heart emptied of worldly desire, even though the original narrative concerns material provision.

paragraphs.text: Pri Tzaddik, Tetzaveh 6 — “Amalek 'dwells in the land of the Negev.' The Gemara says of 'You have given me the land of the Negev': 'A house dried out of every good thing ... a person who possesses nothing but Torah.' Amalek dwells there: he enters the heart of a holy person emptied of all the delights of this world, possessing nothing but Torah. It is like the serpent coming to entice Adam, who was emptied of worldly desires, as it says, 'They were not ashamed,' for he knew nothing of desire. He was in the Garden of Eden, the place of His Divine Presence, yet the serpent entered and enticed him. This is Amalek's kelipah, the beginning and root of the kelipos, opposing the holy beginning.” The cited earlier maamar spells out the Negev analogy and connects the possibility of temptation in an otherwise pure heart to Adam's original situation.

paragraphs.text: Avos 2:4 — “Hillel says: Do not separate yourself from the community. Do not trust yourself until the day of your death. paragraphs.text: Chagigah 15a — “He said: 'Since that man has been driven out of that world, let him go out and enjoy this world.' Acher went out to a life of wrongdoing. paragraphs.text: Rashi on Ezekiel 8:17; Targum Yonasan on Ezekiel 8:17 — “'They put forth the zemorah to their nose': They send to their own nostrils the bad smell of this zemorah, making music with the wind issuing from the anus. That is, this shame of theirs will return upon their faces. Menachem explains the expression as a matter of disgrace and dishonor. ... Their backs being turned to Hashem's sanctuary indicates the matter.” Rashi connects the verse to a deliberately contemptuous bodily gesture. The Targum renders the conclusion more generally: 'They bring shame upon their faces.' Thus the Targum supports the language of disgrace, while the explicit bodily explanation is Rashi's.

paragraphs.text: Kiddushin 30b — “The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel: 'My children, I created the evil inclination and I created Torah as its remedy. If you occupy yourselves with Torah, you will not be delivered into its hand, as it says, If you do well, shall it not be lifted up? But if you do not occupy yourselves with Torah, you are delivered into its hand, as it says, Sin crouches at the door. Moreover, all its occupation is with you, as it says, Its desire is toward you. If you wish, you can rule over it, as it says, You shall rule over it.'” The source couples the reality of the inclination with a divinely provided means of resistance. Rav Tzadok further explains the energy of desire as capable of being directed toward yearning for Torah.

paragraphs.text: Sukkah 52a — “Rabbi Avira expounded—or some say Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: The evil inclination has seven names. paragraphs.text: Sukkah 52a — “Abaye heard a man say to a woman: 'Let us rise early and go on the road.' He said: 'I shall go and separate them from a prohibition.' He followed them for three parasangs through the marsh. When they parted, he heard them say: 'The road is long, but our company was pleasant.' Abaye said: 'Had it been me, I could not have restrained myself.' He went and leaned upon the doorpost, distressed. An elder came and taught him: 'Whoever is greater than his fellow has an inclination greater than his fellow's.'” The story supplies the setting of Abaye's admission: the couple separated innocently, while he recognized the danger he himself might have faced. The elder's answer explains why greatness and strong temptation can coexist.

paragraphs.text: Pri Tzaddik, Terumah 8 — “Yetzer means yearning: Hashem created the person with desire and longing rooted within him, and the choice is given to him to direct that longing toward holiness or, Heaven forbid, its opposite. ... This is the purpose for which the inclination was created: that there should be desire and yearning for Torah. 'If this repulsive one encounters you, draw him to the study hall' means drawing the longing so that it becomes yearning for Torah. Therefore, one greater than his fellow, because yearning for Torah is rooted more strongly within him, encounters a stronger opposite longing as well, for God made the one corresponding to the other.” The earlier passage explains the causal connection in the Sukkah saying: stronger spiritual longing carries an opposing possibility. It does not identify the intensity of temptation by itself as a proof of spiritual attainment.

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 118b — “Rav Yehudah said in Rav's name: Had Israel observed the first Shabbos, no nation or tongue would have ruled over them, as it says, 'On the seventh day some of the people went out to gather,' followed by 'Amalek came.' Rabbi Yochanan said in Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai's name: If Israel observed two Shabbosos according to their laws, they would be redeemed immediately, as it says, 'Thus says Hashem to the eunuchs who keep My Shabbosos,' followed by 'I shall bring them to My holy mountain.'” The first statement supplies the connection between Shabbos and Amalek; the second explains why Shabbos can also be presented as the route to immediate redemption. Rav Tzadok understands the lasting subjugation as the later fruit of the inward damage Amalek introduced.

paragraphs.text: Joshua 2:11 — “We heard, and our hearts melted; no spirit remained in anyone because of you, for Hashem your God is God in the heavens above and on the earth below.” Rachav reports the continuing terror of Israel's God. Rav Tzadok uses her words to show that Amalek's attack did not immediately remove Israel's manifest military and spiritual power; the subjugation described by the Gemara therefore calls for a deeper explanation.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Shem MiShmuel, Vayakhel — “They were drained of vitality, did not believe in themselves, and were like those in despair… and through this loss of inner vitality Amalek gained power to draw them out from beneath the clouds.” The Sochatchover’s reading adds that despair is the inner flaw through which Amalek rules, whether it comes first or Amalek implants it. He finds the same pattern in Haman’s “yeshno am,” a people asleep and despairing of redemption.

paragraphs.text: Eruvin 54a — “Rav Acha bar Yaakov said: No nation or tongue would have ruled over them, for it says, 'Engraved'—do not read charus, engraved, but cheirus, freedom.” The Gemara discusses what would have followed had the first tablets not been broken. Rav Tzadok relates this freedom from foreign domination to the state Israel could have retained at the giving of the Torah.

paragraphs.text: Yoma 38b — “Reish Lakish said: What is meant by 'If it concerns scoffers, He scoffs; to the humble He gives grace'? One who comes to become impure is given an opening; one who comes to become pure is given assistance.” This is the precise rabbinic wording behind the final assurance of assistance. The person's beginning toward purity matters even where the complete overcoming of Amalek requires help from above.
